title: What happens if you add a `NOT NULL` constraint to a column that already contains NULLs (error — you must backfill first), and how do you do it safely on a large table (add column nullable → backfill in batches → add NOT NULL)?
shortTitle: Adding NOT NULL to a Column That Already Contains NULLs
topicTitle: What happens if you add a `NOT NULL` constraint to a column that already contain

s1_definition.profdef: Adding a `NOT NULL` constraint to a column that already contains null values fails with an error, because the constraint would be immediately violated by the existing nulls. The constraint can only be added once every row has a non-null value. On a large table the safe procedure is a multi-step, zero-downtime migration: add the column as nullable (or leave the existing column nullable), backfill the nulls with a value in small batches to avoid a long lock and bloat, and only then add the NOT NULL constraint — using NOT VALID plus VALIDATE where the database supports it to avoid a full-table lock.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India decides every account must now record a branch code, but millions of old accounts have that field blank. If you declare "branch code can never be blank" immediately, the database refuses because all those old blanks already break the new rule. The safe way is to first allow blanks, then quietly go through the old accounts a few thousand at a time filling in their branch code, and only once none are blank do you stamp the rule "branch code is mandatory."
s1_definition.oneliner: NOT NULL on a column with existing nulls errors out; add the column nullable, backfill the nulls in small batches, then enforce NOT NULL.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Adding a `NOT NULL` constraint to a column that already contains null values fails with an error, because the constraint would be immediately violated by the existing nulls. The constraint can only be added once every row has a non-null value. On a large table the safe procedure is a multi-step, zero-downtime migration: add the column as nullable (or leave the existing column nullable), backfill the nulls with a value in small batches to avoid a long lock and bloat, and only then add the NOT NULL constraint — using NOT VALID plus VALIDATE where the database supports it to avoid a full-table lock.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India decides every account must now record a branch code, but millions of old accounts have that field blank. If you declare "branch code can never be blank" immediately, the database refuses because all those old blanks already break the new rule. The safe way is to first allow blanks, then quietly go through the old accounts a few thousand at a time filling in their branch code, and only once none are blank do you stamp the rule "branch code is mandatory."

**One line to remember:** NOT NULL on a column with existing nulls errors out; add the column nullable, backfill the nulls in small batches, then enforce NOT NULL.

sections.s2_technical:
When you run ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL (or add a NOT NULL column without a default), the database validates that no existing row violates the rule. If any row holds a null in that column, the statement fails immediately with a not-null violation. There is nothing subtle here: the constraint is a promise about all rows, and the engine will not accept a promise that the current data already breaks.

The naive fixes are dangerous on a large table. Adding a NOT NULL column with a non-null DEFAULT used to rewrite the entire table and hold a strong lock for the whole rewrite, blocking reads and writes; modern PostgreSQL optimizes a constant default so it is fast, but a volatile or computed default still rewrites. A single huge UPDATE to backfill every null at once takes a long lock, generates enormous write-ahead log and undo, and can bloat the table and block other transactions for minutes.

The safe, zero-downtime procedure has three phases. Phase one, add the column as nullable (or ensure the existing column stays nullable) so the schema change is instant and nothing breaks; deploy application code that starts writing a value into the column for all new and updated rows. Phase two, backfill the historical nulls in small batches — update a few thousand rows at a time in a loop, each batch its own short transaction, with a brief pause so vacuum and replication keep up; this spreads the lock and the write-ahead log over time instead of one giant hit. Phase three, once a query confirms zero remaining nulls, add the NOT NULL constraint. In PostgreSQL you can add a CHECK (column IS NOT NULL) as NOT VALID first — which takes only a brief lock and does not scan existing rows — then run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT to verify existing rows without blocking writes, and finally promote it; this avoids the full-table exclusive lock that a direct SET NOT NULL scan would take on older versions.

The senior nuance is ordering this with application deploys so there is never a window where new rows can still be written as null before the constraint lands, and choosing the backfill value carefully — a static default, a computed value from other columns, or a lookup — while monitoring replication lag and lock waits throughout.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India adds a mandatory branch_code to the large accounts table, but millions of existing rows have it null. A direct NOT NULL fails and a single giant UPDATE would lock the table.

Problem 1 — the direct constraint errors. We show adding NOT NULL while nulls exist throwing a violation.

Problem 2 — batched backfill. We backfill nulls a few thousand at a time in separate short transactions, so no single operation holds a long lock.

Problem 3 — safe promotion. Only after zero nulls remain do we add NOT NULL, modelling the NOT VALID then VALIDATE approach.

The code models a BigTable with many null branch codes, a SchemaMigrator that performs the failing direct attempt, a batched backfill, and the final constrained promotion, with a demo running the whole sequence.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
notnull-migration-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/main/java/com/bank/nnmig/
│   ├── NotNullMigrationDemo.java
│   ├── db/BigTable.java
│   └── migrate/SchemaMigrator.java
└── src/main/resources/db/migration/
    ├── V2__add_branch_code_nullable.sql
    ├── V3__backfill_branch_code.sql
    └── V4__branch_code_not_null.sql
```

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V2__add_branch_code_nullable.sql — Phase 1: instant, nullable
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN branch_code VARCHAR(10);   -- no default, nullable, fast

-- V3__backfill_branch_code.sql — Phase 2: batched backfill (run in a loop/job)
-- UPDATE accounts SET branch_code = 'DEL001'
--   WHERE branch_code IS NULL AND id IN (
--     SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE branch_code IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000);
-- repeat until 0 rows updated; each batch is its own short transaction.

-- V4__branch_code_not_null.sql — Phase 3: enforce without a long lock
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT chk_branch_not_null CHECK (branch_code IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE accounts VALIDATE CONSTRAINT chk_branch_not_null;   -- validates existing rows, no write-block
ALTER TABLE accounts ALTER COLUMN branch_code SET NOT NULL;     -- now safe; can drop the CHECK after
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
migration:
  batch-size: 5000
  pause-ms: 50           # breather so vacuum/replication keep up
  default-branch: DEL001
```

```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests
# Run
java -cp target/notnull-migration-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.nnmig.NotNullMigrationDemo

```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: an accounts table with 12,000 rows, all with a null branch_code, and a batch size of 5,000.

Step 1 — The wrong way: the migrator immediately tries SET NOT NULL. Because 12,000 nulls exist, the database rejects it with a not-null violation. Nothing is changed and the error is logged.

Step 2 — The right way, phase one: the column is already nullable, so new and updated rows begin carrying a value (in the model the table simply holds nulls to be filled). The count of nulls before backfill is 12,000.

Step 3 — Phase two: the backfill runs in batches of 5,000 in a loop. The first batch fills 5,000, the second another 5,000, and the third the final 2,000, after which a batch fills zero and the loop stops. Each batch is a short, independent transaction, so no single operation holds a long lock or produces a huge write-ahead log.

Step 4 — Phase three: with zero nulls remaining, SET NOT NULL now succeeds. In real PostgreSQL this is done via a CHECK IS NOT NULL added NOT VALID then VALIDATEd to avoid a full-table write lock. The column is now mandatory and the migration completed with no downtime.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 17:45:00 [INFO] === WRONG: direct NOT NULL on a table full of nulls ===
2026-10-25 17:45:00 [SEVERE] direct SET NOT NULL failed
2026-10-25 17:45:00 [INFO] === RIGHT: add nullable → backfill in batches → enforce ===
2026-10-25 17:45:00 [INFO] nulls before backfill: 12000
2026-10-25 17:45:00 [INFO] backfill complete in 4 batches; nulls now 0
2026-10-25 17:45:00 [INFO] NOT NULL enforced on branch_code
2026-10-25 17:45:00 [INFO] NOT NULL enforced? true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Goal: make branch_code NOT NULL on a 200M-row table
    │
    ├─ WRONG: ALTER ... SET NOT NULL now
    │    └─ existing nulls → ERROR (not-null violation), table unchanged
    │
    └─ RIGHT: three phases, zero downtime
         Phase 1: ADD COLUMN branch_code (nullable)        ← instant; app starts writing value
            │
            ▼
         Phase 2: backfill in batches of 5000 (short txns)  ← spreads lock + WAL over time
            │ repeat until remaining nulls = 0
            ▼
         Phase 3: CHECK(branch_code IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID
                  → VALIDATE CONSTRAINT → SET NOT NULL      ← no long write-block
            │
            ▼
         branch_code now mandatory
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
If I try to add a NOT NULL constraint to a column that already contains null values, the statement fails immediately with a not-null violation. That is because the constraint is a promise about every row in the table, and the database will not accept a promise that the current data already breaks. So the constraint can only go on once every row has a non-null value.

On a small table I would just backfill and add the constraint, but on a large table the naive approaches are dangerous. A single huge UPDATE to fill all the nulls at once takes a long lock, generates an enormous amount of write-ahead log and undo, and can block other transactions for minutes, and on older engines adding a NOT NULL column with a computed default rewrote the entire table under a strong lock. So I use a three-phase, zero-downtime migration. Phase one, I add the column as nullable, which is instant, and I deploy application code that starts writing a value into it for every new and updated row, so the set of nulls can only shrink from here. Phase two, I backfill the historical nulls in small batches — a few thousand rows per short transaction in a loop, with a brief pause so vacuum and replication keep up — which spreads the lock and the log over time instead of one giant hit. Phase three, once a query confirms zero nulls remain, I add the constraint; in PostgreSQL I prefer adding a CHECK that the column is not null as NOT VALID first, which takes only a brief lock and skips the existing-row scan, then run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT to verify the old rows without blocking writes, and finally promote to SET NOT NULL.

In our National Bank of India system we made branch_code mandatory on an accounts table with hundreds of millions of rows exactly this way: added it nullable, shipped the app change to populate it, backfilled in five-thousand-row batches overnight while watching replication lag and lock waits, and only then enforced NOT NULL through the NOT VALID and VALIDATE path — all with no downtime and no customer impact. The one thing I sequence carefully is the application deploy, so there is never a window where new rows can still be written null before the constraint lands. The line I remember is that NOT NULL on a column with existing nulls errors out, so I add the column nullable, backfill the nulls in small batches, and only then enforce NOT NULL.
